_check.37: 6.1 · The Five Commitments | C1  I Know

10.label: Same evidence, different conclusions
10.text: When two groups read the same evidence and reach opposite conclusions, the difference usually sits in the interpretive framework each brings to it. Every strategic assessment is shaped partly by the evidence and partly by the assumptions of the people assessing it. Honest strategy separates the two. Use this with “The way we think”.

11.label: The urge to be seen doing something
11.text: Under pressure, the most dangerous leadership reflex is the urge to be seen to be doing something. The discipline to slow down, think clearly and act from assessed calm is one of the rarest leadership capacities. Use this to show System 1 under pressure.

11.label: The considered word
11.text: Authority makes a leader’s snap judgements louder than intended. Before endorsing a direction in the room, build in a deliberate pause (“let me sit with that and come back to you tomorrow”) so people act on the considered judgement. Use this to show System 2 as a leadership habit.

12.label: Knowledge, capability and wisdom
12.text: Organisations can hold deep technical expertise and still make poor choices when judgement lacks the discipline of purpose. Fragmentation around personalities distorts collective direction. Use this with the six partial readings of the elephant: each expert is accurate about their part.

13.label: The person who does not fit the template
13.text: A team that is too uniform will be blind to the moments it was never built for. When building a team, deliberately include the person who does not fit the template; that person often solves the problem no one else can see.

14.label: Overconfidence after a win
14.text: Overconfidence after a significant victory is one of the most dangerous leadership conditions. Build a habit of consultation that holds regardless of how strong the last result felt.

14.label: Committing before counting the cost
14.text: The leader who promises the board a delivery date in the heat of the meeting, or announces a pricing change before the commercial modelling is done, shows the planning fallacy at work. One discipline: no public commitment to a number, date or outcome above an agreed threshold without a 24-hour pause.

15.label: Engineered blind spots
15.text: A leader who fills the room with people who agree has engineered a blind spot and called it harmony. Unwelcome accuracy is worth more than pleasant confirmation. Seek out the person willing to say what the agreeable majority will not, and protect them from the cost honesty usually carries. Use this with Groupthink and Authority.

15.label: Informal pressure
15.text: Informal social pressure can overpower formally held beliefs. No policy is needed; the presence of particular people is enough to change behaviour. This is culture operating through signals, belonging and perceived approval. Use this with Conformity.

19.label: Complementary capability
19.text: Sustainable execution rarely depends on one dominant function. Value is produced when differentiated capabilities are deliberately integrated around a common purpose. Use this with “Does my ‘Done’ actually create more work for you?”

22.label: Deciding first
22.text: Organisations often decide first and then use analysis to validate the decision. Sound strategy needs enough humility to let evidence alter the chosen path. Use this with Confirmation bias in Phase 1.

22.label: Disciplined diagnosis
22.text: Consequential decisions require leaders to separate facts from framing, individual interests from institutional interests, and genuine risk from manufactured urgency. Use this across Phases 1 and 2.

23.label: The sunk-cost trap
23.text: Organisations often continue weak initiatives because money, reputation or effort has already been invested, defending yesterday’s choice at the expense of tomorrow’s outcome. Sound strategy needs the courage to discontinue an unsuitable course, absorb the immediate cost and return to the principles that should govern the decision.

23.label: Outcomes taken as proof
23.text: Senior teams routinely read good outcomes as evidence of sound process. A deal closes or a launch lands, and the messy path that produced it is quietly adopted as the method. Ask participants to pick one recent win and audit how it happened separately from what it produced. Use this with Phase 4 · Execution.

24.label: Fear-Dominated
24.text: A technically correct leader can still generate fear, silence or defensive behaviour through the way they exercise authority. Leaders need to examine what their habitual responses create around them, alongside what their decisions accomplish.

24.label: Narcissism-Dominated
24.text: When advisers reinforce the posture the leader already wants to adopt, the leadership team becomes an echo chamber. People learn that influence is gained through agreement, and the culture loses the ability to challenge damaging assumptions.

24.label: Grounded Confidence
24.text: In a crisis, organisations with a culture of calm, evidence-based thinking hold their nerve better than those that follow the emotional temperature of the room. Build the capacity for calm assessment before you need it.

25.label: Psychological Safety
25.text: Part of an organisation’s culture is what people believe will happen to them if they try something and it fails. Where the prevailing belief is that failure is punished, people stop trying, whatever the stated values say. Examine what people saw happen to the last person who took a risk and got it wrong.

25.label: Morale Drain
25.text: Cultures become healthier when people can voice concern, disappointment or uncertainty without being labelled negative or disloyal. Suppressed emotion moves underground.

26.label: Principle 3 · Designated challenger
26.text: Most flawed plans survive because dissent was quietly designed out of the room. Before the next significant decision, invite the one person most likely to disagree and hear them out fully.

26.label: Verification before response
26.text: A common and costly strategic failure is acting at the speed of assumption on information that was heard and never confirmed. Build an explicit verification step into decision-making before any significant response.

29.label: Cognitive Integration
29.text: The most accurate intelligence about what the organisation’s decisions are producing is often held by those furthest from the decision-making centre. Build explicit structures that bring this intelligence from the edges into the rooms where decisions are made.

29.label: Behavioural Guardrails
29.text: Leaders who decide by who is loudest in the room, ahead of what is most true in the data, consistently make poor calls. Good judgement goes beneath the surface presentation and the political pressure to what is actually true.

30.label: Blind Ideation · Halo Effect
30.text: Cultures become vulnerable when prestige determines whose ideas matter. Healthy cultures combine competence with humility and value overlooked contributors.

30.label: Insight from every level
30.text: Leaders who assume strategic insight belongs only to the senior tier miss what the rest of the organisation sees. The next strategic insight may come from the youngest person on the team.

31.label: Strategic Post-Mortems
31.text: Shame is what cultures produce when failure is punished and never processed. When people are more afraid of being found wrong than of being wrong, they hide problems until those problems become crises. Build a culture where people can say “I got this wrong” before it becomes “we failed”.

31.label: Public Cognitive Humility
31.text: Teams that only ever hear the polished version stop believing any of it. Name one of your own missteps openly to the people you lead; the candour builds the credibility that spin erodes.

37.label: C1 · I Know My Biases
37.text: Leaders need mechanisms that reveal their blind spots as well as their strengths. Acknowledging difficulty deepens trust when it comes with responsibility, learning and perseverance.
